description: Real incidents hit and resolved building and operating the Self-Healing DB Agent. Kept as a living postmortem log, separate from runbooks.json (what the agent itself consults mid-incident).

incidents.title: Oracle unreachable after every VM reboot (V$ grants wiped)
incidents.problem_statement: /tick returns {"outcome":"oracle_unreachable","detail":"Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)"} immediately after the Oracle VM starts or restarts.
incidents.root_cause: The oracle-xe container is declared via gce-container-declaration with no persistent data volume, so every VM boot reinitializes Oracle as a brand-new database from scratch -- wiping the V$SESSION / V$SYSMETRIC / ALTER SYSTEM grants executor_sa needs. Toolbox returns the resulting ORA-00942 as a plain-text error body, which the client fails to JSON-parse, surfacing as the generic-looking 'Expecting value' message.
solution_steps: SSH into the Oracle VM and locate the running container: docker ps --filter name=klt-oracle-xe.
Run the grant script as SYS: ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=XEPDB1; GRANT SELECT ON V_$SESSION, V_$SYSMETRIC, V_$INSTANCE, V_$VERSION TO executor_sa; GRANT ALTER SYSTEM TO executor_sa;
Confirmed durable fix: the VM startup script re-applies this automatically on every boot (idempotent), retrying the real grant command itself until its own output is clean of ORA-/SP2- errors.

incidents.title: Grant script fails: "No such container: oracle-xe"
incidents.problem_statement: The automatic (or manual) grant-reapplication script errors with Error response from daemon: No such container: oracle-xe.
incidents.root_cause: GCE's Konlet mechanism, which launches containers from a gce-container-declaration block, does not name the real Docker container after the spec's name: field -- the actual name is klt-<name>-<random 4-char suffix>, regenerated fresh on every boot.
solution_steps: Never hardcode the container name.
Look it up dynamically at runtime: ORACLE_CONTAINER=$(docker ps --filter "name=klt-oracle-xe" --format "{{.Names}}" | head -n1).
Use $ORACLE_CONTAINER in every subsequent docker exec.

incidents.title: Intermittent ORA-12514 during the grant fix
incidents.problem_statement: The grant script occasionally fails with ORA-12514: TNS:listener does not currently know of service requested in connect descriptor, even though Oracle is clearly up.
incidents.root_cause: A probe-then-real-command pattern (test connectivity with a disposable connection, then run the real SYS grant as a separate step) raced Oracle's own PDB service registration with the listener: the probe caught a brief window where XEPDB1 was reachable, then the real command ran moments later against a listener that had not finished registering the PDB service yet.
solution_steps: Do not use a separate readiness probe.
Retry the REAL target command itself in a loop, checking its own output for ORA-/SP2- error codes (sqlplus can exit 0 even when individual statements failed).
Back off ~10s between attempts; first-boot registration lag was observed up to a few minutes on e2-medium.

incidents.title: Agent detects real incidents but always returns no_action_proposed
incidents.problem_statement: Sense and Predict correctly detect a confirmed anomaly (e.g. active_blocked_sessions >= 8, sustained), but the Reason stage always ends in {"outcome":"no_action_proposed"} -- the model never calls any tool, with no guardrail or audit trail explaining why.
incidents.root_cause: The ADK agent's McpToolset (the LLM's only path to its remediation tools) was connecting to the bare Toolbox base URL with no path, while Toolbox's actual MCP endpoint lives at /mcp/. Every session-creation attempt failed with a flat 405 Method Not Allowed, silently leaving the agent with zero tools -- invisible from the API response, only visible in raw Cloud Run application logs.
solution_steps: Point the MCP connection at {TOOLBOX_URL}/mcp/, not the bare base URL.
To catch this class of bug earlier: exercise the real Sense->Predict->Reason->Act path at least once per deploy, not just the guardrail-gate demo shortcuts (which bypass the LLM agent entirely).

When outcomes look suspiciously silent, pull raw textPayload logs (gcloud logging read ... AND textPayload:*) rather than trusting the BigQuery audit trail alone -- some failure paths never write an audit row.

incidents.title: GRANT silently mangled: "V_$SESSION" became "V_"
incidents.problem_statement: A grant statement appears to run without error, but the privilege never actually applies -- the executed SQL was silently GRANT SELECT ON V_ TO executor_sa.
incidents.root_cause: Single quotes cannot nest in bash. Inlining a quoted heredoc (<< 'SQL' ... SQL) inside an already single-quoted sudo bash -c '...' wrapper breaks the outer quoting, so $SESSION gets expanded as an (unset, empty) shell variable instead of staying literal.
solution_steps: Never inline a quoted heredoc inside a single-quoted sudo bash -c wrapper.
Write the SQL to a real file first, then reference it with plain file redirection: sqlplus ... < grant_v_views.sql.
When in doubt, cat the file back out immediately after writing it, and diff against the intended content before running it.

incidents.title: sqlplus one-liner fails: ORA-00933 / SP2-0306
incidents.problem_statement: A quick diagnostic query piped in as echo "SELECT ...; EXIT;" | sqlplus fails with ORA-00933: SQL command not properly ended.
incidents.root_cause: A single-line echo with two statements separated only by "; " does not reliably split into separate lines the way sqlplus expects -- it can be read as one malformed statement.
solution_steps: Use printf with explicit \n newlines instead of a single-line echo.
For anything longer than 1-2 statements, prefer a heredoc or a real .sql file over piped echo/printf entirely.

incidents.title: Uploaded script fails with $'\r': command not found
incidents.problem_statement: A shell script that worked when pasted directly fails after being downloaded and re-uploaded, with errors like invalid option and $'\r': command not found on nearly every line.
incidents.root_cause: The file picked up Windows-style CRLF (\r\n) line endings somewhere in a download/upload round-trip -- bash only expects LF (\n) and treats the stray \r as part of the command.
solution_steps: Strip the stray carriage returns before running: sed -i 's/\r$//' script.sh.
Re-run chmod +x if needed, then execute normally.
Prefer pasting directly into Cloud Shell's built-in code editor over a download/upload round-trip when line-ending corruption is a risk.

incidents.title: AlloyDB tools return "Tool ... not found" even after AlloyDB is READY
incidents.problem_statement: /database/info?db=alloydb and any alloydb_* tool call return {"error":"Tool 'alloydb_describe_database' not found."}, persisting even after the AlloyDB instance reaches READY state (confirmed not a startup-timing issue).
incidents.root_cause: database.tf's metadata_startup_script bakes tools_db/tools.yaml into the Oracle VM via Terraform's file() interpolation and rewrites it on every boot, but its sed substitution block only resolves ${ORACLE_*} placeholders -- it never adds the five ${ALLOYDB_HOST}/${ALLOYDB_PORT}/${ALLOYDB_DATABASE}/${ALLOYDB_USER}/${ALLOYDB_PASSWORD} lines. Toolbox loads the file with those placeholders still literal, so the alloydb-db source block (and every tool depending on it, including alloydb_describe_database) silently fails to register -- Oracle tools load fine, masking the gap.
solution_steps: Confirm it is not a timing issue: check gcloud alloydb instances list shows STATUS=READY, then re-curl -- if the error persists, it is the sed gap, not startup lag.

Temporary fix (safe, no Terraform apply): build a fully-resolved tools.yaml locally with BOTH Oracle and AlloyDB placeholders substituted, gcloud compute scp it to the VM, then docker restart toolbox -- confirm via logs it reports the full tool count (e.g. 'Initialized 19 tools') including alloydb_describe_database.

This temporary fix lives only on the VM disk and silently reverts on the next Oracle VM stop/start or reboot, since the startup script unconditionally overwrites tools.yaml from stale Terraform-baked metadata every boot -- re-apply after every restart until the permanent fix ships.

Permanent fix: add the 5 missing ${ALLOYDB_*} sed -e lines to database.tf's metadata_startup_script and apply deliberately with a VM snapshot first -- changing metadata_startup_script forces full VM replacement, so this must never go through a rushed terraform apply.
